content: Approximately 10% of pregnancies are complicated by the passage of meconium during delivery. This can lead to meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS), a condition that may cause respiratory complications and, in rare cases, death. Antibiotics are often prescribed to neonates exposed to meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) to prevent infections that could arise from potential bacterial contamination. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antibiotics in two specific scenarios: (1) preventing infection, illness, and death in neonates born through MSAF who show no symptoms at birth, and (2) preventing infection, illness, and death in neonates born through MSAF who exhibit clinical signs of MAS. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed, including MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, covering studies up to July 2016. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles were also examined. Only randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials were included, while non-randomized studies, cohort studies, and case-control studies were excluded. The review included studies involving both term and preterm neonates and considered any type of antibacterial antibiotic. No language restrictions were applied. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed by reviewing published reports and, when necessary, by contacting study authors directly. Data on relevant outcomes were extracted, and effect sizes were calculated using risk ratios (RRs), risk differences (RDs), and mean differences (MDs). Subgroup analyses were conducted to separately evaluate the use of antibiotics for MAS treatment and for prophylaxis in asymptomatic neonates exposed to meconium. Four randomized controlled trials involving a total of 695 neonates met the inclusion criteria. Three of these studies focused on neonates with MAS, while one study examined asymptomatic neonates exposed to MSAF. The methodological quality of the studies varied: two were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the other two had an unclear risk of bias. The overall quality of evidence was graded as low due to several factors, including high rates of participant loss to follow-up in one trial, small sample sizes across all trials, and insufficient methodological details in two studies. The primary outcome of interest was the risk of earlyand late-onset neonatal sepsis. Among neonates diagnosed with MAS, antibiotics did not significantly reduce the risk of sepsis (RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.27 to 8.96; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.03; 445 participants, three studies; I² = 0%). Similarly, in asymptomatic neonates exposed to MSAF, antibiotics did not significantly lower the risk of sepsis (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.34; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.04; 250 participants, one study; I² = 0%). No significant differences were observed in mortality rates or hospital length of stay between neonates who received antibiotics and those in the control groups, regardless of whether they were symptomatic or asymptomatic. However, one study involving asymptomatic neonates reported a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation in the control group compared to the antibiotic group (MD 0.26, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.37; 250 participants, one study; I² = 0%). In conclusion, the available evidence does not support a reduction in infection rates with the use of antibiotics in neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, whether they are asymptomatic or have MAS. The overall quality of evidence is low due to the limited number of studies and their methodological limitations. Further well-designed and adequately powered studies are needed to provide more definitive answers.
